title: Infra GPU Fleet: Capacity, CI/CD, and IaC Runbook
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview:

This runbook consolidates operational guidance, Terraform/IaC module expectations, CI/CD build patterns, cloud account & networking requirements, and capacity planning processes for Redwood's GPU fleet. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners who operate the Dedicated and Private inference fleets.

Sections:
1) Goals and scope
2) Ownership and SLAs
3) Fleet architecture and capacity targets
4) Cloud accounts & networking baseline
5) Terraform/IaC module patterns and repo layout
6) CI/CD and build pipeline standards
7) Day-2 ops / runbooks (incidents & routine ops)
8) Capacity planning and forecasting process
9) Appendices (commands, module table, escalation matrix)

1) Goals and scope
- Provide a single-source-of-truth for provisioning, scaling, and operating GPU-backed inference capacity.
- Cover cross-cutting requirements: VPC/networking, IAM, billing tags, telemetry, and compliance guardrails.
- Describe standardized Terraform module interface and CI/CD flow for infra changes.
- Include runbooks for common incidents (OOM, node failures, AZ/network degradation, capacity exhaustion).

2) Ownership and SLAs
- Primary owner: infra-gpu team (pager: infra-gpu-oncall).
- Secondary support: eng-sre for escalation on SLOs and incident coordination.
- Target SLOs for Dedicated fleet:
  - Control plane availability: 99.95% monthly
  - Provisioning latency (new pool ready): <= 20 minutes (warm images)
  - Scheduling failure rate: <0.5% of requests
- Cost SLOs (observability goal): maintain median util >= 70% for committed pools and <40% waste on reserved machines.

3) Fleet architecture and capacity targets
- Instance classes: rtx-a800 (inference-heavy), a100-80gb (high-memory models), t4 (low-cost embeddings).
- Pool types: dedicated (reserved), burst (spot preemptible), isolated (private customer VPC).
- Typical pool sizing guidance:
  - Small pool: 4 GPUs (dev / low-throughput workloads)
  - Medium pool: 32 GPUs (standard model serving)
  - Large pool: 128+ GPUs (high-throughput customer commit)
- Autoscaling: horizontal scale by node group with cooldown 3m, scale-down grace 15m, target CPU/GPU utilization triggers configured in autoscale policies.

Capacity target table (monthly planning):
| Pool type | Baseline commit (GPU) | Target util % | Safety buffer (GPUs) | Notes |
|-----------|-----------------------:|-------------:|---------------------:|-------|
| Dedicated | 512                   | 70%          | 20%                  | Reserved for enterprise customers |
| Burst     | 256                   | 50%          | 30%                  | Spot-backed, auto-evict on preemptions |
| Private   | varies                | 75%          | 10%                  | Customer-managed network constraints |

4) Cloud accounts & networking baseline
- Minimum account controls for any GPU account:
  - Organizational tagging: team, cost_center, environment, owner
  - Centralized IAM roles: infra-gpu-admin, infra-gpu-operator, infra-gpu-readonly
  - VPC requirements: dedicated subnet per pool, /26 recommended per node group to allow rolling upgrades and ephemeral pods
  - Private endpoints: control plane must use private link where supported for Private deployments
  - Egress policy: restrict model artifact egress to approved S3 buckets and artifact registries

Networking checklist (before provisioning pool):
1. Verify VPC CIDR has at least /26 free for new node group.
2. Confirm route table and NAT/Gateway configuration for required outbound access (artifact registry, image repo).
3. Ensure NACLs and Security Groups allow SSH from bastion and control-plane subnets only.
4. Validate private link endpoints for control-plane APIs where required by customer.

5) Terraform / IaC module patterns
- Repo layout (recommended):
  - infra/modules/gpu-node-group (reusable module)
  - infra/modules/networking (vpc, subnets, routes)
  - infra/environments/<account>/<region>/main.tf (composition)
  - infra/live (terragrunt wrapper for environments)
- Module interface (gpu-node-group) required inputs:
  - name (string)
  - instance_type (string)
  - gpu_count_per_node (number)
  - desired_capacity / min_size / max_size (numbers)
  - subnet_ids (list)
  - iam_role_arn (string)
  - image_id (string)
  - preemptible (bool)
- Module outputs (standardized):
  - node_group_id
  - instance_profile_arn
  - autoscaling_policy_name
- Best practices:
  - Keep modules small and composable.
  - Enforce tagging and billing_tag propagation inside modules.
  - Use remote state with locking (S3 + DynamoDB) or supported backend.
  - Lock provider versions and module versions in registries.

6) CI/CD and build pipeline standards
- Pipeline components for infra change (recommended):
  1. Preflight: terraform validate, tflint, checkov (security scanner), tfsec
  2. Plan: terraform plan with workspace-specific vars, upload plan artifact
  3. Review: PR must include plan URL and impact summary (changes to GPU counts, instance types, subnets).
  4. Approvals: staging infra change requires 1 approver; production requires 2 approvers including an infra-gpu owner.
  5. Apply: apply runs in a gated runner with MFA-brokered service account.
  6. Post-apply: smoke tests (health checks, telemetry ingestion, node readiness).
- Pipeline runners: dedicated runner pool with AWS role chaining. Avoid running terraform applies from ephemeral developer workstations.
- Image build & artifact registry:
  - Use immutable image tags (sha).
  - Store GPU AMIs/container images in central registry (ECR/GCR) with lifecycle rules and vulnerability scanning.
  - Image promotion flow: build -> scan -> sign -> promote to prod repo.

7) Day-2 ops / Runbooks
A) Capacity exhaustion (hot path)
1. Detect: alert "pool-utilization-critical" when queued requests > 5% of capacity for > 2m.
2. Immediate mitigation:
   - Increase pool desired_capacity by +20% via autoscale policy override if allowed.
   - If reserved capacity exhausted, enable burst pools (spot) and notify sales/customer-success for potential throttling policy.
3. Post-incident:
   - Run cost/usage analysis for 30d window; update monthly forecast.
   - Create follow-up action to add warm pools or increase commit if repeat.

B) Node OOM / CUDA failures
1. Detect: node-level GPU OOM logs, container restarts > 3 in 5m, or kernel oops.
2. Triage:
   - Collect dmesg, nvidia-smi output, container logs, pod yaml.
   - Check GPU driver and CUDA versions against supported matrix (Appendix B).
3. Mitigation:
   - Drain and cordon the node, roll impacted workloads to healthy nodes.
   - If driver-level issue, initiate node-bounce using image with previous known-good driver.
4. Postmortem: tag failure with model, image, and scale pattern for regression monitoring.

C) AZ / network degradation
1. Detect: increased pod evictions, cross-AZ latency spikes, or control-plane session errors.
2. Steps:
   - Shift traffic away from impacted AZ via routing policy or spin up additional nodes in healthy AZs.
   - If cross-region failover required, follow Disaster Recovery Runbook (link in related pages).

8) Capacity planning and forecasting process
- Cadence: monthly forecast cycle and quarterly capacity review for major model launches.
- Inputs to forecast:
  - Historical token throughput by model and route (30/90/180 day windows)
  - Sales/CS customer commitments pipeline (expected start date and committed GPUs)
  - Planned product launches and A/B tests with projected load
  - Observed tail-latency patterns and eviction rates
- Process steps (monthly):
  1. Infra-gpu owner collects telemetry exports and a utilization heatmap.
  2. Run the baseline growth model (current runrate * growth factor + buffer).
  3. Tag any forecasted risk windows (holidays, product launches).
  4. Generate procurement request for cloud reserved instances or commit plans.
  5. Publish plan to infra roadmap and notify Finance for budget adjustments.

9) Appendices
A: Common CLI commands
- Terraform plan: terraform plan -var-file=env/prod.tfvars -out=plan.tfplan
- Apply (CI only): terraform apply "plan.tfplan"
- Check node status: kubectl get nodes -l pool=gpu -o wide
- Drain node: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data

B: Supported driver matrix (summary)
- CUDA 12.1 + Driver 535.x: supported for a100 and RTX-A series images
- CUDA 11.8 + Driver 510.x: supported for legacy a100-40gb and t4 images

C: Terraform module inventory
| Module | Repo | Owner | Required inputs (short) | Notes |
|--------|------|-------|-------------------------|-------|
| gpu-node-group | infra/modules/gpu-node-group | infra-gpu | name,instance_type,gpu_count_per_node,desired_capacity,subnet_ids,iam_role_arn,image_id | Standard nodegroup with autoscale hooks |
| networking | infra/modules/networking | infra-network | vpc_cidr,azs,public_subnet_prefixes,private_subnet_prefixes | VPC composition and NACL defaults |

D: Escalation matrix
- Pager: infra-gpu-oncall -> if unresolved 30m -> eng-sre-oncall -> if unresolved 2h -> infra-eng manager -> exec on-call as per incident policy.
